01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: What is the objective of software engineering, as defined in the course?
options: To write code as quickly as possible
To move from a vaguely described real system to a very specific computerized system
To document every requirement before any design starts
To replace business analysts with developers
01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.explain: SE moves from a real system described ambiguously in plain language to a computerized system written very specifically in a programming language.

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: Which three broad activities take you from the real system to the computerized system?
options: Requirements & Analysis → System & Object Design → Implementation & Testing
01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.explain: The three broad activities are Requirements & Analysis, System & Object Design, then Implementation & Testing. Real projects loop back rather than moving linearly.

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: In the SDLC, which phase answers the question "What needs to be done?"
01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.explain: Elicitation + Analysis = what; Design = how; Implementation = do it; Testing = verify it does what it's supposed to.

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: Why is the SDLC called a cycle rather than a line?
options: Because it is repeated once per year
Because the real process loops back between stages rather than running straight through once

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: Requirements Engineering is made up of which two activities?
01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.explain: Requirements Engineering = Elicitation + Analysis. It overlaps heavily with Business Analysis when the solution is to create or update software.

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: Which development model is described as an ad hoc loop with no planning or design phase?
01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.explain: Build-and-fix: Build → Use → Fix → Use → … → Retirement.

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: When does the waterfall model actually work well?
options: When requirements are expected to change frequently
When the team has never worked in the domain before
When you are confident you fully understand the requirements, or the client has given them unambiguously
When the system must be delivered in short releases
01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.explain: Its two problems: understanding of the problem may stay unclear until late, and the problem itself may change over time.

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: In the incremental model, each new increment is layered on top of a shared…
What distinguishes evolutionary prototyping from throw-away prototyping?
options: Evolutionary prototypes are drawn on paper
Each system version is built with the intention of evolving into the next, rather than being discarded
Evolutionary prototyping skips the requirements phase entirely
Evolutionary prototypes are only used for technical feasibility

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: Which pair of process models does the course say are, from a process point of view, already agile methods?
options: Evolutionary prototyping and the incremental model
01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.explain: Agile methods reduce risk by delivering software in short releases — evolutionary prototyping and incremental already do that.

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: Which is NOT one of the four Agile Manifesto value pairs?
options: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Following a plan over responding to change
01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.explain: It's the other way round: responding to change over following a plan.

01-intro-to-sdlc-and-agile.q: According to the Agile principles, what is the primary measure of progress?
The Agile principle of "simplicity" is described as…
options: Using the simplest programming language available
Maximizing the amount of work not done
Having only one developer per feature

02-requirements-elicitation.q: Which definition of a requirement matches the course?
options: A line of code that must compile
A feature the system must have, or a constraint it must satisfy, to be accepted by the client
A test case written by QA
A deadline set by the project manager
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: BABOK v3 frames it more broadly as a usable representation of a need. At its core, a requirement addresses a problem or an opportunity.

02-requirements-elicitation.q: MoSCoW analysis is a technique for…
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: Must have / Should have / Could have / Won't have.

02-requirements-elicitation.q: BABOK v3 groups requirements into which four categories?
"Increase revenue by accepting credit-card payments before Dec. 31st" is an example of a…
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: Business requirements are high-level organizational goals and should be measurable and time-bound.

02-requirements-elicitation.q: Solution requirements split into which two categories?
"The system must be deployed as a Docker container" is what type of requirement?
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: Transition requirements describe how the solution is deployed/released — temporary capabilities like migration, data conversion and training.

02-requirements-elicitation.q: "Ability to search by product code, name, or category" is a…
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: FRs describe required behaviours of the solution, usually from the system's perspective.

02-requirements-elicitation.q: "Restore service within 1 hour of an outage" describes which quality attribute?
"Support 1,000 simultaneous users and keep 5 years of historical data" is which NFR attribute?
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: Capacity = the amount of data or services the solution can manage. Scalability is about growing to meet increased demand (e.g. 2× volume).

02-requirements-elicitation.q: Which is NOT another name for non-functional requirements?
Which elicitation technique is especially good for uncovering tacit requirements people struggle to put into words?
You need input from 5,000 users quickly, including demographic data. Which technique fits best?
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: Surveys quickly solicit information from a large number of users using closed- or open-ended questions.

02-requirements-elicitation.q: Which technique convenes stakeholders in a structured session to reconcile differences and reach consensus?
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: Focus groups gather prequalified participants for qualitative attitudes/expectations; facilitated workshops aim at consensus and resolving conflicts.

02-requirements-elicitation.q: What is the main risk of document analysis?
options: Working from documentation that is outdated or inaccurate
It only works for system-replacement projects
It cannot be used early in a project
How users, processes and other system components interact, including each interfacing system's input/output needs
The look and feel of competitor products
Stakeholders' emotional reactions to a prototype

02-requirements-elicitation.q: Why record who said what during interviews?
options: So the interview can be structured

02-requirements-elicitation.q: Which is NOT one of the elicitation success factors?
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: The five: preparation, active stakeholder engagement, defined business/organizational need, domain knowledge, and a plan for the elicitation.

02-requirements-elicitation.q: In an adaptive (agile) life cycle, when does elicitation happen?
options: Only at the start, until the solution is fully defined
Continuously, alongside analysis, one iteration at a time
Only after the product is released
02-requirements-elicitation.explain: Predictive: as early as possible, producing formal specs. Adaptive: continuous, producing lightweight docs like user stories / backlog.

03-requirements-analysis.q: What does Requirements Analysis (BABOK: Specify and Model Requirements) produce?
options: Specifications and models representing the elicitation results

03-requirements-analysis.q: In the course's framing, verifying requirements makes sure they meet ____, while validating makes sure they satisfy ____.
options: the business goals; the stakeholders' needs
the stakeholders' needs; the business goals
the code standards; the test cases
03-requirements-analysis.explain: Verify → stakeholders' needs. Validate → business goals.

03-requirements-analysis.q: When should traceability information be included?
options: While creating the models/artifacts, not afterwards

03-requirements-analysis.q: Starting from a requirement, you want to find every test case and design element built on it. That's…
03-requirements-analysis.explain: Forward = everything that depends on it. Backward = everything it depended on (its sources). Bidirectional = both.

03-requirements-analysis.q: What is the purpose of a requirements glossary?
options: To list all the developers on the project
To limit the vocabulary and reduce ambiguity
03-requirements-analysis.explain: It defines business-specific terms and links synonyms (e.g. customer/client/shopper). CoreX takes it further as a controlled vocabulary with no synonyms.

03-requirements-analysis.q: Which are the five CoreX models?
options: Domain, workflow, data (entity), business rules, conceptual UI design
Use case, class, sequence, state, activity

03-requirements-analysis.q: Which CoreX model is the only one that is NOT visual?
Which CoreX model is the only one tied to a target platform (GUI, touch, speech, IVR)?
The lecture's rule of thumb for progressive decomposition is…
options: Up to three levels, with 4 or 5 elements at each level
03-requirements-analysis.explain: The CoreX reading says Level 1 ≈ 3–8 concepts, each decomposed into another 3–8; deeper levels can grow (10–15) but not excessively.

03-requirements-analysis.q: Which tool is most popular for building the domain model?
Where does the scope of the application get drawn in CoreX?
options: In the domain model — the covered region is shaded, everything outside is out of scope

03-requirements-analysis.q: The workflow model models the system's ____, while the data model models its ____.
03-requirements-analysis.explain: Workflow = behaviour (simplified UML activity diagram). Data = structure (simplified class/ER diagram).

03-requirements-analysis.q: In a CoreX workflow model, which symbol is "not likely to be needed at this level"?
In the workflow model, how should an activity be named?
options: As a verb + noun, e.g. "Create groups"

03-requirements-analysis.q: In CoreX's NAVA scheme, verbs and adverbs go into which model?
03-requirements-analysis.explain: Nouns + adjectives → entity/data model (tables, fields). Verbs + adverbs → workflow model (buttons, links, command options).

03-requirements-analysis.q: In CoreX's entity model rules, how are relationships and entities expressed?
options: All entities are plural and all relationships are many-to-many; cardinality goes in the business rules model
Cardinality is shown on every relationship line

03-requirements-analysis.q: "Loans of $100,000 or more must be approved by a senior officer" belongs in which model?
03-requirements-analysis.explain: Business rules cross-bind data, workflow and UI so the right people do the right activities on the right data at the right time.

03-requirements-analysis.q: Mapping CoreX to MVC: the Controller corresponds to…
options: The workflow model + business rules model
03-requirements-analysis.explain: Model ≈ entity model, Controller ≈ workflow + business rules, View ≈ user interface.

03-requirements-analysis.q: Work requirements in CoreX come from which technique?
03-requirements-analysis.explain: JAD defines a job's KRAs, KPIs, KTs and competencies.

04-work-items.q: What is the correct hierarchy of work items, from largest to smallest?
In the online-store example, "Shopping Cart" is a(n)…
04-work-items.explain: Online-Store is the epic, Shopping Cart is the feature, and "As a shopper I would like to delete an item from my cart" is a user story.

04-work-items.q: Which level of the work-item hierarchy is optional — some teams skip it?
An epic can be seen as either a logical grouping of related user stories or…
options: a big user story that needs to be broken down

04-work-items.q: Which level of work items is outside the scope of SE 3352?
Which is the user story template?
options: As a ⟨type of user⟩, I want ⟨goal⟩ so that ⟨some reason⟩.

04-work-items.q: What is the Definition of Done for a user story?
options: The date the story is due
The list of conditions (acceptance test) the story must meet to count as complete
The developer assigned to the story
04-work-items.explain: It guides testing and is what makes a story Testable under INVEST. Writing it surfaces hidden prerequisites (e.g. account + login for RSS).

04-work-items.q: What does the "N" in INVEST stand for, and what does it mean?
options: Necessary — the story is legally required
Negotiable — captures the essence of the need and leaves room for conversation, not a contract
Numbered — each story has an ID
New — the story hasn't been built before

04-work-items.q: Per INVEST, how small should a story be?
A story is ____ if it can be released without depending on other stories.
Why might you write user stories instead of use cases early in an agile project?
options: Use cases are not allowed in agile
Use cases are formal analysis models, and the detail needed to write them often isn't available yet
User stories are more detailed than use cases

04-work-items.q: From Mike Cohn's example backlogs, which statement is true?
options: Every example story passes all of INVEST
Non-functional requirements can also be written as user stories
Stories must never contain open questions
04-work-items.explain: E.g. a user wanting fast responses or Unicode support. Roles also go beyond "user" — editor, admin, trainer, even a search engine.

04-work-items.q: Which is NOT one of the ways the course says you can look at user stories?
options: One of the models used in requirements analysis
A replacement for all non-functional requirements

05-analytical-skills.q: What is analytical skill, as defined in the course?
options: The ability to write code without bugs
The ability to deconstruct information into smaller categories in order to draw conclusions
The ability to think quickly under pressure
The ability to imagine what is not there

05-analytical-skills.q: According to Richard J. Heuer Jr., how do analysts learn to think analytically?
options: By doing — it's a skill that improves with practice
It is innate and cannot be learned

05-analytical-skills.q: Caroselli's three critical thinking categories are…
Which thinking category contemplates "what is not there"?
05-analytical-skills.explain: Analytical = what IS there (linear, logical). Creative = what is NOT there (non-linear).

05-analytical-skills.q: What does the course say about quick thinking?
options: It is sufficient on its own
Speed is necessary but not sufficient — it must be backed by analytical or creative thought
It is the same as creative thinking

05-analytical-skills.q: The word "critical" comes from the Greek krisis, meaning…
Organizing everything you see in a picture into a 3-level hierarchy practices the same skill as building which model?
In the ATM class diagram exercise, Savings Account and Current Account are most naturally grouped as…
05-analytical-skills.explain: Both are types of Account, which groups them into one level of the simplified data model.

05-analytical-skills.q: Coming up with three different ways to break "Fill Order" into sub-steps practices decomposition for which model?
Describing LinkedIn in terms of epics, features and user stories practices…
options: Organizing concepts into the work-item hierarchy

06-prototyping.q: Steve McMenamin's quote "Prototypes are requirements bait" means…
options: Prototypes trick stakeholders into signing contracts
Stakeholders react readily to something concrete, which surfaces the real requirements

06-prototyping.q: Which is NOT one of the uses of a prototype listed in the course?
Why generate several sacrificial (throw-away) candidate solutions?
options: One candidate isn't enough to open your mind; comparing many reveals the real requirements
Because the first prototype is always wrong
To choose the cheapest one immediately
06-prototyping.explain: "If you want to have a good idea, have lots of ideas." — Linus Pauling

06-prototyping.q: How much should a low-fidelity sketch show?
options: As much of the business as is needed to understand the problem — the wider ecosystem, not just a screen

06-prototyping.q: In the customs example, which is the wireframe?
options: A drawing of a truck approaching a scanner and an officer deciding
A screen with Truck ID, Manifest ID, Origin, Destination, contents and a "Stop and Inspect" button
A video of the border crossing
A mind map of customs concepts

06-prototyping.q: A sequence of panels showing a candidate solution in use, scene by scene with text under each, is a…
06-prototyping.explain: Borrowed from film. Example: the home security solution with Brad and Janet.

06-prototyping.q: Which prototype type combines drawing and text, branching out from one central concept?
Why is a process model good for presenting a candidate solution?
options: Its notation (rectangles + arrows) is simple enough that almost any stakeholder can grasp it immediately
It is the only model that can be usability tested

06-prototyping.q: An LMS dashboard designed in Figma that looks real but doesn't work is a…

options: Describing desired behaviour to an AI coding assistant, generating a working version, and refining iteratively
Designing every class and API up front

06-prototyping.q: Which caveat does the course give about vibe-coded prototypes?
options: They are a proof of concept only — needing significant re-engineering for production — and you shouldn't send private data/ideas to an LLM without a reliable privacy agreement
They can't be shown to stakeholders
They must be written in Python

06-prototyping.q: Which question does the course suggest asking stakeholders about a prototype?
options: How many lines of code is this?
Is this addressing all of the problem?
What color should the buttons be?
06-prototyping.explain: Others: why would this solve your problem? how would it affect the rest of your business? does it suggest some other solution?

final.q: A hospital asks for software but can only describe its problem vaguely. Moving from that description to a precise program is…
A client hands you a complete, unambiguous spec for a payroll system that won't change. Which model is most defensible?
final.explain: Waterfall works when you're confident you fully understand the requirements or they've been given unambiguously.

final.q: The SDLC phase System Design + Object Design answers which question?
options: Is it doing what it's supposed to?

final.q: Which Agile principle conflicts most with a team that only demos software once a year?
options: Deliver working software frequently (weeks, not months)

final.q: "The LMS must authenticate all users via SSO." What type of requirement and attribute is this?
"The LMS must stay usable when enrolment doubles next year while still meeting performance targets." Which NFR attribute?
"Instructors must be trained on the new grading module, and old grades must be migrated before launch." This is a…
"Mean time between failures shall not exceed X" describes…
"Prompt users to confirm financial transactions after entering details" is an example of which attribute?
Which requirement category provides the basis for identifying solution requirements by expressing the needs of a specific group?
PMI adds project, quality and program requirements. How does the course treat them?
options: As part of project/program work owned by the PM, not the requirements process
As a replacement for BABOK categories

final.q: You're replacing a 15-year-old registration system and want to keep what works and drop what doesn't. Best technique?
Warehouse staff can't explain how they actually pick orders — they "just know." Best technique?
Your system must exchange data with the provincial health registry. Which technique identifies its input/output needs and interoperability issues?
Sales and Finance disagree on the discount workflow. You need them to reach consensus early. Best technique?
An interview where questions are prepared in advance but you follow up freely based on answers is…
Which elicitation success factor is about deciding stakeholders, session order and how to conduct sessions before starting?
"Not all requirements are known at the start, so elicitation is iterative" is the idea of…
final.explain: Progressive elaboration (PMI) is about requirements emerging over time; progressive decomposition (CoreX) is about building models top-down with level caps.

final.q: A test fails and you need to know which business need and stakeholder the requirement came from. Which traceability direction?
Which is a recommended practice for traceability according to the course?
options: Keep all traceability in one giant document
A spreadsheet matrix, or metadata in tools like Jira/Confluence; avoid forcing one giant document
Traceability is only for waterfall projects

final.q: In an e-commerce app, stakeholders use "customer", "client" and "shopper" for the same thing. What should the glossary do?
options: Keep all three as separate concepts
Link them as synonyms and settle on one term
Make each a separate entity in the data model

final.q: CoreX comes from which point of view?
In CoreX's three-step process, what is the first step?
options: Requirements gathering — define the problem (via JAD)

final.q: Which CoreX key principle helps avoid legacy thinking?
options: Give people exactly what they say they want

final.q: What does CoreX do with non-functional requirements?
options: Converts them into functional ones (KPIs, best-practice workflow, UX) the team is accountable for
Puts them all in the glossary

final.q: In CoreX co-design, the analyst drafts models to about Level 2 before a workshop. How are those drafts used?
options: Only to restart a stalled session or to compare — the group builds the models from scratch
Emailed to stakeholders instead of holding a workshop

final.q: From the requirement "Instructors grade submitted assignments promptly", which word lands in the workflow model?
final.explain: Verbs (grade) and adverbs (promptly) → workflow model. Nouns (Instructors, assignments) and adjectives (submitted) → entity model.

final.q: In a GUI built from CoreX models, nouns and adjectives typically become…
"An Olympic athlete can only play a sport for one country" — in the CoreX entity model, how is this cardinality shown?
options: As a one-to-one line between Athletes and Countries
It isn't — relationships stay many-to-many and the constraint goes in the business rules model

final.q: Which business-rule category covers "which roles may perform which tasks on which data"?
Why keep business rules in one model instead of in UI code or the database?
options: It makes rule interactions visible and lets rules change at run time, instead of hiding them deep in code
Because the database can't store rules

final.q: In the data model at Level 1, a box like "Regulated parties"…
options: May become a package or component rather than an entity/class

final.q: The conceptual UI design is compared to an architect's…
final.explain: Enough to confirm the concept with decision-makers before detailed design; usually key workbenches plus screens for key workflows, and usability-testable.

final.q: On the conceptual UI example, the top navigation tabs trace back to which model?
final.explain: Domain → navigation tabs; data → tables of records; workflow → Update/Manage controls; business rules → constraints like the running total.

final.q: In the student-groups workflow, "Groups are joinable?" with Yes/No branches is drawn as a…
CoreX leaves which of these OUT of the workflow model?
Which user story best follows the template and INVEST?
options: Build the database schema for carts.
As a shopper, I want to delete an item from my cart so that I only pay for what I want.
As a developer, I want to rewrite the entire site.

final.q: A story would take the team three sprints. Which INVEST criterion does it most clearly fail?
A story has no acceptance criteria, so nobody can confirm when it's finished. Which INVEST criterion fails?
Writing the Definition of Done for "subscribe to an RSS feed" revealed that users also need an account and a login. This shows the DoD…
In Mike Cohn's example backlogs, notes like "After each survey? After a set period?" illustrate which INVEST idea?
options: Negotiable — the story is a placeholder for a conversation

final.q: For an LMS, "Course Catalog", "Quizzes" and "Forums" groupings in a backlog act like…
College students need textbooks. You sketch five very different ways (bookstore, second-hand, print-on-demand, espresso printer, tablet download). This is…
Sally's Freecycle chair example — Sally joins → takes photos → posts → time passes → applicant responds → pickup — is shown as a…
"Good Food for One" with branches for recipes, search, meal of the day, and profile is an example of a…
Which prototype is built with the organization's programming languages and actually works?
Why might you present a candidate solution as a video walk-through?
options: People are visual and drawn to moving images, making it an engaging way to show how a solution would work

final.q: Which thinking category is linear and logical, analyzing what is there?
Mock-ups/wireframes sit at the overlap of which areas?
options: Elicitation, analysis and interface design (design thinking)

final.q: Work requirements map to the job. If part of the job has no matching requirement, what happens?
options: People can't do that part of their job in the app
